narrative: Global markets are navigating sharp cross-currents driven by a deepening tech correction, tumbling energy prices, and high-stakes US midterm elections. The Nasdaq 100 slid into correction territory, down 10% from its October high, as hedge funds de-gross and investors penalize massive AI capital expenditures lacking near-term monetization. In contrast, crude oil plunged 3% to 6% as reports that President Donald Trump is pursuing diplomacy with Iran eased immediate Middle East strike fears and energy disruption premiums. US equity sentiment is attempting a fragile stabilization, with analysts viewing the midterms as a potential clearing event that could release sidelined capital despite political gridlock risks. Meanwhile, sticky US inflation metrics and expectations of restrictive central bank policy continue to anchor bond yields near recent highs.

Nasdaq.view: The index entered correction territory down 10% from its October peak, pressured by record hedge fund selling, AI monetization doubts, and mixed earnings from Apple and Palantir.

S&P 500.view: Mike Wilson of Morgan Stanley views the midterm elections as a clearing event and a dip-buying opportunity targeting 8,000, while easing oil prices help broaden market participation beyond mega-cap tech.

Gold.view: According to Bloomberg's Anthony Stephens, gold broke below key technical support at $4,000 and remains vulnerable due to an unusually high correlation with falling tech stocks during portfolio de-grossing.

Oil.view: WTI and Brent dropped 3% to 6% toward $100-$106 per barrel as geopolitical supply risk unwound on reports that Trump is prioritizing diplomatic talks with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

priced_in: An 80-85% probability of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December 2026.
A Bank of England rate hike on Thursday driven by surging energy costs.
Midterm election consensus favoring a divided government or Democratic sweep (Kalshi odds ~71-72%).
Aggressive AI CapEx spending models that punish revenue misses.
Partial de-escalation of the Middle East geopolitical risk premium following Iranian diplomatic proposals.
debates: Mike Wilson (Morgan Stanley) sees midterms as a clearing event to buy dips toward 8,000, whereas Howard Marks (Oaktree) warns the AI 'bubble of infallibility' has burst amid deteriorating credit conditions.
Derek Halpenny (MUFG) sees USD vulnerable to AI momentum slowdowns, while Mark McCormick (BMO) maintains a bullish dollar view on US economic outperformance and rate differentials.
Jeff Currie (Real Macro) argues structural supply redundancy will keep deferred oil prices high, while anchors point to immediate near-term crude collapses on US-Iran diplomacy.

Paul Donovan (UBS) characterizes the tech sell-off as an earnings reassessment rather than a macro warning, while Violeta Todorova (Leverage Shares) warns of severe vulnerability as chip indices enter bear market territory.
